topic.en: Three texts: cities uncovering buried rivers, what goes on inside a sourdough starter, and the argument about returning museum objects.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: қалалар көмілген өзендерді қалай ашады, ашытқының ішінде не болады және мұражай заттарын қайтару туралы талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: как города откапывают засыпанные реки, что происходит внутри закваски и спор о возврате музейных предметов.

paragraphs.text: Almost every old city is built over water it can no longer see. The stream that decided where the first houses stood, that turned the mills and took away the waste, is usually still there, running in a brick pipe a few metres below the pavement. London has dozens of them; so do Vienna, Boston and Seoul. For a century and a half they were treated as plumbing rather than as rivers, and a generation of engineers grew up who had never seen the water they were managing. The recent argument about digging some of them up again is therefore not really an argument about landscape. It is an argument about what a city thinks a river is for.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The reasons for burying them were good ones at the time. An open stream in a crowded nineteenth-century city was a sewer in everything but name, and the link between filthy water and disease was becoming impossible to ignore. A covered channel could be flushed, it did not smell, and it could not be used as a rubbish tip. There was a second motive that is less often mentioned in the official histories: burying a stream freed land for building, and land in the middle of a growing city was the most valuable thing a council owned. A culvert could carry a road, a market or a row of shops on its back.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The modern reversal began in the 1990s, and the project everyone cites is in a capital in East Asia. A stream that had been covered in the 1950s and roofed with an elevated motorway was reopened along almost six kilometres of the city centre. The motorway was taken down, the concrete lid was lifted, and a channel with walkways on both banks was opened in 2005 at a cost of several hundred million dollars. The scheme was fiercely opposed by drivers and by shopkeepers along the route, and it is now the example that every other city points at when it wants to make the same argument.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: What the measurements show is more interesting than the photographs. Along the restored corridor, summer air temperatures fell by about three degrees compared with streets a few blocks away, because moving water and the breeze it draws behave like a long thin park. Counts of birds, fish and insects rose from almost nothing to figures comparable with a small nature reserve. Footfall in the surrounding streets increased, and so, predictably, did rents. Traffic, which everyone had expected to seize up when the motorway went, largely disappeared instead: drivers who lost the route made other journeys or made none.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The flood argument is the one that convinces engineers. A pipe has a fixed capacity, and when a storm exceeds it the water comes up through the manholes with nowhere to go. An open channel can rise, slow down and spread into the ground beside it, and a restored stream with a shallow floodplain will hold a great deal of rain that a culvert simply delivers to the next bottleneck. This only works if the water is clean, which is why daylighting is usually carried out together with work to separate sewage from rainwater. Done carelessly, in the wrong part of a catchment, reopening a channel can move a flood rather than absorb it.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of this is cheap, and the objections are not foolish. Land must be bought or taken, traffic must go somewhere, and the work is measured in years of closed streets. Critics also point out where the gains land: property beside a restored stream rises in value, and the people who lived next to the culvert when it was an eyesore are often the first to be priced out of the view. A city that reopens a river without building housing at the same time has, in effect, spent public money to raise private rents.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The test of a restored stream is whether it is a river or a water feature. Some celebrated projects are kept flowing by pumped water, drawn from elsewhere and pushed along a decorative channel, which is an expensive fountain rather than a returning ecosystem. The schemes that work are the ones connected to a living catchment: a real flow with a real source, fish that can swim up it, and banks that can flood without anyone panicking. That is harder, slower and less photogenic than lifting a concrete lid, and it is the only version that keeps paying after the ribbon is cut.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: A sourdough loaf is made from flour, water and salt, and that is the whole ingredient list. What is missing from it is the packet of dried yeast that most bread depends on. The rising is done instead by a starter: a paste of flour and water kept on a kitchen shelf and fed regularly, in which wild yeasts and bacteria live together in large numbers. A baker who keeps a starter is farming a small ecosystem rather than adding a chemical, and the difference shows up in the taste, the texture and the time the bread takes to make. The practice is far older than the science: bread was being raised this way for thousands of years before anyone knew what was doing the raising.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The inhabitants of a starter fall into two groups that need each other. The yeasts, which are not the same species as commercial baker’s yeast, break down sugars and release carbon dioxide, and it is this gas, caught in the dough, that makes the loaf rise. Alongside them live lactic acid bacteria, ten or more of them for every yeast cell, which produce the acids that give sourdough its name. The acids lower the pH of the dough, and the low pH suits the yeasts while discouraging most of the organisms that would otherwise spoil the mixture. Each group makes the environment more comfortable for the other, which is why a well-fed starter is remarkably difficult to kill.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Acidity does more than provide a flavour. Bread spoils in two ways, by going stale and by going mouldy, and the acids attack the second. A loaf raised with a starter typically resists mould for several days longer than an equivalent loaf made with commercial yeast, which is the reason sourdough was the ordinary bread of Europe for centuries before refrigeration. The same acids act on the flour itself. They activate an enzyme that breaks down phytic acid, a compound in wholegrain flour that binds iron and zinc and carries them out of the body unused, so a long sourdough fermentation makes more of those minerals available to the person eating the bread. Bakers noticed the keeping quality long before anyone could explain it, and built their working week around it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Time is the other ingredient. A commercial loaf can be mixed, raised and baked in under three hours; a sourdough is usually left for somewhere between twelve and twenty-four hours, most of it in a cool place. During that slow fermentation, enzymes and bacteria take apart some of the long protein chains in the flour, including fragments that are difficult for some people to digest. Studies of people with mild wheat sensitivity — though not of those with coeliac disease, for whom no bread of this kind is safe — have found that a long-fermented loaf causes fewer symptoms than a fast-risen one. The gluten is not removed, but it is partly dismantled before it is eaten.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Does the bread taste of the place it is made? Bakers like to say that a starter picks up the character of its city, and the claim has been tested. When researchers gave identical flour and identical instructions to bakers in different countries and then analysed the starters they produced, the communities of microbes turned out to differ, but they did not group by geography in the way the story predicts. What mattered more was the baker: the temperature of the kitchen, the flour used before the experiment began, how often the starter was fed, and even the microbes on the baker’s own hands. A starter is shaped by a household rather than by a climate.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Most bread sold as sourdough in supermarkets is not made this way. Industrial bakeries work to timetables that a twelve-hour fermentation cannot fit, so a common practice is to raise the dough with commercial yeast and add a powdered acid or a small quantity of dried starter for flavour. The result rises on schedule and tastes faintly sour, but it has not been fermented long enough to gain any of the advantages described above, and it goes mouldy on the ordinary timetable. Several countries have considered rules about what may be called sourdough, and a few have passed them; in most markets the word still means whatever the label wants it to mean. For a shopper the only dependable signal is the ingredient list: flour, water, salt and a starter, with nothing after them.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The great museums of Europe and North America were assembled during the century when their countries governed much of the world, and the collections show it. A significant proportion of the objects in them left their place of origin in circumstances that no modern museum would accept: taken as spoils after a punitive raid, bought for a token sum from someone who had no right to sell, or removed by an expedition whose permit had been granted by an occupying power. For most of the twentieth century this was treated as an awkward historical footnote. It is now the central question the institutions face, and the arguments on each side are better than the shouting suggests. The four positions set out below belong to people who have spent their working lives inside the dispute, and none of them is the caricature that the other side tends to answer.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Sofia Renner, who has advised several national collections, makes the case that has come to be called the universal museum. An object seen beside things from four continents tells a different story from the same object in a room of its neighbours, and there is a public good in a place where a visitor can walk between civilisations in an afternoon. Break the great collections up, she argues, and nothing equivalent can be rebuilt; a hundred complete national collections would still not contain a single room in which the world could be compared with itself. Her position is not that acquisitions were fair, but that dismantling the result destroys something the original wrong did not create. She adds that the question is being decided object by object, which suits newspapers and suits nobody else.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Kwame Bediako answers that this argument has the question backwards. Whatever the value of a comparative collection, he writes, it cannot be built out of other people’s property and then defended on the grounds that it would be a pity to take it apart; the same reasoning would justify keeping anything sufficiently well displayed. The people from whom the objects were taken never agreed to the exchange, and their descendants are asked to accept a benefit they did not choose in place of a thing they did not sell. What is owed is not access but the object, and the decision about where it is displayed belongs to its owners. If those owners then choose to lend it back, he notes, that is an agreement rather than a concession.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Helena Marsh approaches it as a practical matter of what the law allows. Most national museums are bound by statutes that forbid them to give away anything in their care, drafted long before restitution was contemplated and designed to stop trustees selling the collection to cover a deficit. Where governments have wanted returns to happen they have had to pass fresh legislation, which several have now done, and where they have not, curators who agree with the principle can do very little. Long-term loans have been used as a way round the rule, but a loan leaves ownership where it was, which is precisely the point at issue. Her advice to campaigners is to read the founding statute of the institution before writing to its director.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Ibrahim Nasser is impatient with a claim that is often made quietly in defence of delay: that returned objects would be poorly cared for. He points to purpose-built museums in Lagos, Dakar and Mexico City with climate control and conservation laboratories, and notes that the great collections themselves lose objects to theft, fire and water. The argument was never really about shelving, he suggests. It is about who is assumed to be a competent custodian, and that assumption has been revised everywhere except in the sentences of those who are still deciding.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What has actually changed is smaller than the speeches and larger than nothing. Several governments have passed laws allowing returns, a number of high-profile objects have gone home, and the burden of proof has quietly reversed: a museum now explains why it is keeping a contested object rather than waiting to be asked. Most collections, however, remain where they were, and the practical questions — what to do about objects whose origin is disputed between two modern states, or about things acquired legally but under conditions nobody would now call free — have barely been worked out. The honest summary is that the principle is close to settled and the procedure is not.
paragraphs.label: F
